To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) there is an increasing demand for systems engineers in the United States; (b) the current certification process for the professional systems engineer (PSE) is too narrow in its focus; (c) there is no clear consensus among systems engineers on what constitutes a PSE; and (d) there is no consensus on what should be required to obtain a PSE certification.

(a) there is an urgent need for the harmonization and solidification of the BoK requirements of ABET and the IEEE/INCOSE certification of systems engineers; (b) a closer partnership between the three organizations is needed to reach agreement on the BoK requirements for the accreditation and certification of systems engineers at the baccalaurate level, which could be used as a benchmark for the development of Bo Ks for any certification beyond the baccalauareate level.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following: 1) The need for a systems engineering body of knowledge (SEBoK) that is comprehensive and authoritative, and which is accepted by the systems engineering community, including ABET.

the following: (a) the development and use of a systems engineering curriculum framework, (b) the development of an ABET‐compliant curriculum for a systems engineering program, (c) the development and implementation of a systems engineering capstone course, and (d) the use of a systems approach in teaching and learning engineering.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there is a need for a systems engineering certification that is based on an established body of knowledge, that has the support of the professional societies and the accreditation bodies, and that is accepted by the industry and government.
the ABET accreditation process for systems engineering programs is not a substitute for professional certification of systems engineering graduates.
the certification of systems engineering professionals at any level beyond the baccalau­reate level is not a requirement, but is a highly desirable goal.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are in the process of creating a new Systems Engineering Body of Knowledge (SEBoK) that is based on the current IEEE and INCOSE BoKs.
the ABET and IEEE/INCOSE collaboration will lead to a more harmonized and solidified body of knowledge for systems engineering.

we have identified the need to harmonize the requirements and expectations of the two major certification organizations (INCOSE and IEEE) with the accreditation requirements of ABET for the academic‐bachelors degree in systems engineering.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the accreditation of systems programs by ABET and certification of systems engineers by INCOSE and IEEE should be harmonized.
ABET accreditation and professional certification of engineers should not be seen as mutually exclusive.
